headline: MSI and Colorful raise Nvidia RTX 50-series prices in China by up to 59%
summary: Distributor pricing changes suggest GPU price hikes are on the way globally, impacting Nvidia, AMD, and Intel cards.
details: MSI and Colorful have announced new pricing for their entire Nvidia RTX 50-series graphics card lineup in China, with increases of up to 59% compared to MSRP. This move by distributors suggests that GPU price hikes may soon become a global trend, affecting cards from Nvidia, AMD, and Intel.

MSI's price list reveals increases of 10-20% over their previous, already inflated prices. The RTX 5080 Shadow 3X OC/Ventus saw a 20% hike, moving from 10,000 Yuan ($1,477) to 12,000 Yuan ($1,773). Other RTX 5080 variants and RTX 5070 Ti models also experienced significant increases.

Even the higher-end RTX 5090 D V2, a cut-down version of the RTX 5090, saw a 13% price increase. Lower-tier cards like the RTX 5060 and RTX 5050 variants experienced hikes around 14-15%. The RTX 5060 Ti and RTX 5070 saw smaller increases, under 10%.

When compared to the official MSRPs, the price hikes are even more stark. The RTX 5070 Ti Gaming Trio OC is now 76% above MSRP, while the RTX 5090 D V2 is 57.5% higher. Other RTX 50-series cards are also significantly more expensive than their suggested retail prices.

Colorful's pricing also shows substantial increases over MSRP, with the RTX 5080 Vulcan W OC priced at 59% above MSRP and the 5070 Ti Vulcan W OC at 58.5% higher. Many other models from Colorful also exceed MSRP by considerable margins.

The trend isn't limited to Nvidia. AMD cards are selling for 14% to 29% higher prices, and Intel Arc cards are seeing bumps of $200 to nearly $300. The RX 9060 XT 16GB is noted as a particular offender among AMD cards, with an 28.8% increase over MSRP.

These price surges are largely attributed to the skyrocketing cost of VRAM modules, which have reportedly increased by $20 per module. This alone adds approximately $100 to an 8GB card, $130 to a 12GB card, and $180 to a 16GB card, before considering other manufacturing costs and market demand.

With no signs of the component crisis abating, and with companies potentially using fearmongering tactics to encourage immediate purchases, consumers may face persistently high GPU prices for the foreseeable future.
